USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold at the current posture rather than escalate further to the threatened ~$300B tranche. We have just maximally escalated (25% on ~$200B of Chinese goods, plus the May 15 supply-chain executive order), and China has retaliated by raising duties on ~$60B of US goods. Do not fire the $300B arrow; keep the 25% pressure in place as leverage and preserve the resumption path — both sides have already agreed to continue talks and a Trump-Xi G20 meeting is on the calendar for late June. The correct move is to sustain pressure without driving the dispute into a full trade war that would mostly tax our own consumers and farmers.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading (threat_score +0.4) is driven by costs of the escalation now materializing for US interests: the 10-year Treasury yield has fallen from ~3.06% in November to 2.37% by May 15 and the 2-year to 2.16%, a pronounced risk-off signal that markets fear the trade war across a growth slowdown; investors lost roughly $1 trillion in market value on the May 13 rout; and the farm belt — a politically pivotal constituency — has been severely hurt, with Chinese soybean purchases down about 90% and prices near $8/bushel with no resolution in sight. Economists and even the administration's own adviser concede US businesses and consumers bear the tariffs, with Oxford Economics estimating a ~0.3% GDP drag in 2020. These are material economic and political pressures, but not existential: the US controls the escalation lever, unemployment is low, and consumer sentiment stands at 100, so this sits between neutral and high rather than at the existential anchor. The action stance (action_score 0.0, hold) reflects the second-order calculus: escalating to the remaining $300B would cover nearly all consumer goods China exports and would directly tax US households while inviting maximal retaliation, whereas conceding now would abandon the leverage just built and reward Beijing's renegotiation of previously agreed text. Holding the line while keeping the negotiation channel and scheduled G20 meeting open is the disciplined middle path.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain calibrated, proportionate retaliation to the United States' latest escalation while explicitly keeping the negotiating channel open and avoiding any move that would invite the threatened additional ~$300B in tariffs or a broader Huawei-supply-chain ban. We have already raised our retaliatory rates on the ~$60B US-goods list (May 13); the correct posture now is firm, measured reciprocity that signals resolve at home and no unilateral surrender abroad, without stepping onto terrain that deepens full tech decoupling.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high and rising. The US successively raised tariffs to 25% on the entire ~$250B Section 301 tranche (May 10) and directed preparation of tariffs on the remaining ~$300B (May 5) — coverage that would hit essentially all of our exports to the US — and on May 15 signed EO 13873 and moved to place Huawei on the Entity List, direct targeting of our flagship technology firm and Made in China 2025 ambitions (event timeline: 2019-05-05, 2019-05-10, 2019-05-13, 2019-05-15). The yuan has come under real pressure, slumping to a 2019 low of 6.9040 with its worst daily fall in nine months and analysts flagging risk of a breach of the sensitive 7/$ level and capital flight (web: Reuters, 2019-05-13; Yahoo, 2019-05-13). This maps to the +0.5 CHN anchor (major export sectors hit, firm-level Huawei targeting, FX pressure) and tilts slightly higher given the breadth of the escalation, hence threat_score +0.6 — serious but not existential because our reserves remain ample (~$3.095tn) and the dispute also offers a nationalist rallying point and impetus to accelerate tech self-sufficiency. On action: this moment is too dangerous to over-escalate — full retaliation into the remaining $300B threat or a rare-earths/entity-list broadside would likely provoke still-wider US action and accelerate Huawei decoupling, which is exactly what we must not invite; but given the scale of the US escalation and domestic expectations of resolve, unilateral concession is untenable. A calibrated retaliate stance (action_score -0.3) defends our red lines while leaving room to return to the substantive talks that were showing progress as recently as April (event timeline: 2019-04-03).
